title: Hypertension: diagnosing, choosing drugs, and targets

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2017 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline and standard primary care practice. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Under the ACC/AHA definition, at what office blood pressure does stage 1 hypertension begin?
questions.why: Stage 2 begins at 140/90. Elevated blood pressure is a systolic of 120 to 129 with a diastolic under 80.

questions.q: Which classes are first-line for uncomplicated hypertension?
questions.why: Beta blockers are reserved for a compelling indication such as heart failure, prior infarction or rate control; on their own they protect less against stroke.

questions.q: A Black adult with hypertension and no heart failure or kidney disease. Which initial therapy is preferred?
questions.a: A thiazide-type diuretic or a calcium channel blocker
questions.why: Renin-angiotensin blockers lower blood pressure less on average in this group as monotherapy, though they are still used when there is albuminuria or heart failure.

questions.q: Hypertension with chronic kidney disease and albuminuria. Which class should be part of the regimen?
questions.why: The benefit is slowing progression of the kidney disease, which is why it applies with albuminuria even when blood pressure could be controlled another way.

questions.q: What is the blood pressure target for most adults being treated for hypertension?
questions.why: The same target applies in older adults who are living independently; it is relaxed only where the burden of treatment or a limited life expectancy argues for it.

questions.q: When is starting two antihypertensives at once recommended rather than one?
questions.a: Stage 2 hypertension, with blood pressure 20/10 mm Hg or more above target
d: Only when a single drug has failed at full dose
questions.why: Two drugs from different classes, ideally in one pill, get more patients to target and improve adherence. Single-drug starts are for stage 1.

questions.a: An ACE inhibitor with an ARB
d: An ACE inhibitor with a thiazide
A calcium channel blocker with an ARB
A thiazide with a calcium channel blocker
questions.why: Dual renin-angiotensin blockade adds hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without extra cardiovascular benefit. The other three are standard pairings.

questions.q: After starting an ACE inhibitor, up to what rise in creatinine is acceptable without stopping the drug?
questions.why: A modest early rise reflects the drop in glomerular pressure that protects the kidney long term. A larger rise should prompt a look for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

questions.q: A patient on losartan becomes pregnant. What should happen to the losartan?
questions.a: Stop it now and switch to a pregnancy-safe agent
d: Continue it through the first trimester
Continue it; only ACE inhibitors are a problem
questions.why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs both cause fetal kidney injury and oligohydramnios, worst in the second and third trimesters, so the switch happens at the first knowledge of pregnancy.

questions.q: Which antihypertensives are preferred in pregnancy?
questions.why: Labetalol and long-acting nifedipine are the usual first choices; methyldopa is older and safe but weaker. All three renin-angiotensin agents listed are contraindicated.

questions.q: A patient started on amlodipine three weeks ago has new bilateral ankle swelling with no other findings. What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Dihydropyridine oedema comes from arteriolar dilation, is dose related, and does not respond to diuretics. Lowering the dose or adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB helps.

questions.q: Resistant hypertension means blood pressure above goal despite how many drugs at optimal doses, one of them a diuretic?
questions.why: Before calling it resistant, confirm adherence, technique and out-of-office readings, and look for interfering drugs such as NSAIDs and decongestants.

questions.q: Which drug is the usual fourth agent in resistant hypertension?
questions.why: In the PATHWAY-2 trial spironolactone outperformed bisoprolol and doxazosin as the add-on, which fits the excess aldosterone found in many resistant patients.

questions.q: Office readings are consistently high but the patient says home readings are normal. What confirms or refutes hypertension?
questions.a: Out-of-office measurement, by home or ambulatory monitoring
d: A repeat office reading the same day
A single reading taken by a nurse
questions.why: White-coat hypertension is common and carries less risk than sustained hypertension, so treatment decisions rest on out-of-office numbers.

questions.q: After starting or changing an antihypertensive, when should blood pressure be reassessed?
questions.why: A month is long enough to see the full effect of most agents. Once at target, reassessment stretches to every 3 to 6 months.
